title: Pogroms (1881)
hookLine: waves of violence in Russia push Jews to emigrate and to new ideas

lines: A TOWN IN THE OLD COUNTRY.
cards: A town nobody in the family has seen for generations. A grandmother's recipe that came from there, a grandfather's trade, a surname that changed at a border.
Ask a Jewish family in America, or England, or Argentina, why they left that town, and sometimes the answer is one word, a word that came into English from Russian and stayed.
Behind it are towns in the Russian Empire where crowds turned on the Jews who lived there: doors smashed, shops emptied, people hurt and killed.

teach.b: A pogrom is an attack by a crowd on a Jewish community: houses, shops, synagogues and people. In the Russian Empire, waves of them broke out across many towns, and came back again and again over the years that followed.
Laws pressed in at the same time, limiting where Jews could live and what they could do.
One town's name became a byword: Kishinev. After the violence there, the Hebrew poet Hayim Nahman Bialik went to see it. His poem, In the City of Slaughter, is hard to read.
He grieves for the dead. And he turns, angry, on the survivors who hid, and even on heaven, which went on shining as if nothing happened. It is not a comforting poem.
What the history teaches next: people did not answer in one way. Some left, in great numbers, for America and other shores; that is the great wave you met a few days ago.

Some formed groups called Lovers of Zion and began farming villages in the land of Israel. A physician named Leon Pinsker wrote a pamphlet arguing that Jews would not be safe until they had a home of their own.

Some young people organized to defend their streets. Others joined movements that wanted to stay and win equal rights right where they were. Same violence, different answers: leaving, building, defending, organizing.
The days ahead follow some of those roads.
Today, remember that each of these waves fell on real people with names.

how: Jewish communities remember the dead with memorial prayers and by saying 'may their memory be a blessing'; some families keep the stories and photographs of the towns their ancestors left.

some left, some built in the land of Israel, some defended their streets, some organized to win rights at home.
Bialik's poem grieves only for the dead
it grieves, and it also turns in anger on the survivors who hid, and even on heaven.
the word pogrom came into English from Russian
and the attacks it names are part of why many families left the Russian Empire.

games.q: you are a young Jew in a town in the Russian Empire after a wave of attacks. what do you do?
o: the history shows all of these, and more.
games.why: people left, built, defended and organized. the same violence pushed them down very different roads.

practice: You don't need any image of the violence; call up an ordinary street instead, a bakery, a schoolroom, a doorway with a mezuzah, and let it stand for the families who lived in those towns, and for any of your own family who came from far away.
If you pray, ask that their memory be a blessing; if you don't, just hold the street quietly, full of people.

wordCard.voice: Pogrom. An attack by a crowd on a Jewish community, a word that came into English from Russian after waves of them in the Russian Empire. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: real people with names. Every wave of this history fell on a street like that one. That's day nine hundred ninety-eight.
